A2.text:
Kamran's grandmother, Zarifa, was eighty on Sunday. The whole family wanted to buy her gifts. Kamran is a student, and he did not have much money.

His cousin Ramin is rich. He bought Grandma a big new TV. “Grandma will love it,” Ramin said.

Kamran was sad. He wanted to be generous too. Then he had an idea. He wanted to make something thoughtful.

He visited all his aunts and uncles. He asked them for old photos of Grandma and for one story about her. Some stories were funny, and some were very kind. He made a big photo album. It took him three weeks. He wanted to go the extra mile. He wrote all the stories under the photos.

On Sunday, he took time to wrap the album in red paper. He felt a little shy. “It is a small gift,” he said.

Grandma opened the TV box first. “Thank you, Ramin. That is very kind,” she said. Then she opened the album. She read it for a long time and started to cry.

“Kamran, this is the best gift,” she said. “You gave me my whole life.”

Kamran smiled. “I owe you a lot, Grandma,” he said. “Family is give and take,” she answered.

“Remember,” she said, “it's the thought that counts.”

The next week, Grandma decided to donate the big TV to a children's charity. But she kept the album next to her bed.

B1.text:
When Grandmother Zarifa turned eighty, her family planned a big celebration at a restaurant in Novkhani. Zarifa always tried to refuse presents, but everyone was talking about them. Kamran, a second-year student living on a small grant, felt the pressure more than anyone.

His cousin Ramin, who worked for an oil company, announced that he had bought her the largest smart TV in the shop. “Sixty-five inches,” he said proudly.

Kamran couldn't compete with that. For a few days he felt miserable. Then he remembered something his grandmother often said: the best gifts are the ones you can't buy.

He spent the next three weeks travelling across Baku and Sumgait, visiting every aunt, uncle and old neighbour he could find. From each of them, he collected an old photograph of Zarifa and one story. An old colleague remembered how she secretly paid for a young teacher's wedding dress. Kamran scanned the photos, wrote the stories underneath them and had everything printed as a thick album. He really went the extra mile — he even found a picture from her own wedding in 1964.

On the night of the party, he wrapped the album in plain brown paper with a ribbon. Next to Ramin's enormous box, it looked tiny.

Zarifa opened Ramin's gift first and thanked him warmly. “What a generous gesture,” she said. Then she opened the album. She turned the pages slowly, reading every story. The table went quiet. When she looked up, her eyes were wet.

“Who told you about the wedding dress?” she whispered. “I never told anyone.”

“I owe you everything, Grandma,” Kamran said. “I wanted you to know how many people feel the same.”

She held his face in her hands. “It's the thought that counts,” she said. “And this, my dear, is a lot of thought.”

A week later, Zarifa asked Ramin, very politely, if he minded her donating the TV to a children's charity in Sumgait. The album stayed on her bedside table.

B2.text:
Grandmother Zarifa's eightieth birthday was to be celebrated in style — a long table at a restaurant in Novkhani, forty guests, a cake shaped like the house she had lived in for half a century. In the weeks beforehand, the family conversation revolved around one subject: presents. For Kamran, a second-year student surviving on a modest grant, it was a source of quiet dread.

His cousin Ramin, an engineer with an oil company and a talent for being noticed, announced that he had secured the largest television in the shop. “Sixty-five inches,” he said. “She'll be able to follow her series from the balcony.”

Kamran could not compete with that, and for several days he didn't try. Then a phrase surfaced that his grandmother had repeated throughout his childhood: the gifts worth having are the ones that can't be bought.

He spent the next three weeks criss-crossing Baku and Sumgait, tracking down aunts, uncles, former neighbours and colleagues. From each, he asked for two things — an old photograph of Zarifa and a single story about her. A retired colleague confided that Zarifa had once quietly paid for a young teacher's wedding dress and sworn her to secrecy. Kamran scanned every photograph, wrote each story beneath it and had the whole collection bound into a heavy album. He went the extra mile in every sense, at one point taking three buses to a village outside Shamakhi to borrow the only surviving picture of her wedding.

On the night, he wrapped it in plain brown paper and tied it with string. Beside Ramin's colossal box, it looked almost apologetic.

Zarifa opened the television first and thanked Ramin with real warmth. “A very generous gesture,” she said. Then she untied the string. She turned the pages slowly, reading every word, and gradually the table fell silent. When she raised her head, her eyes were bright.

“Who told you about the wedding dress?” she asked softly. “I never told a soul.”

“I owe you more than I can repay, Grandma,” Kamran said. “I just wanted you to see how many people feel the same way.”

She took his face in both hands. “They say it's the thought that counts,” she murmured. “This is a lifetime of thought.”

A week later, with impeccable tact, she asked Ramin whether he would object to her donating the television to a children's charity in Sumgait. The album never left her bedside table.
